screens.title: Secure Software Development Life Cycle (SSDLC)
screens.narratorSegment: We begin by treating security as an integral part of software design rather than an add-on. The Secure Software Development Life Cycle, or SSDLC, shifts security left so that concerns like data protection, threat modeling, and secure defaults are considered from the first requirement and design discussions. This reduces cost and risk because vulnerabilities discovered early are cheaper and simpler to fix than those found in production. In this lesson you will learn what it means to shift left, how to define security requirements that capture data sensitivity and regulatory needs, how designers can apply threat modeling techniques to anticipate attacks, and how development and testing practices catch issues before deployment. A practical example is defining a credential-protection requirement during planning and confirming it in design through threat modeling; that single early decision saves time in later code reviews and penetration testing. A common misconception is that adding a security team late in the cycle is sufficient. In practice, late involvement often creates rework and missed controls. As you go through these screens, ask yourself: which early decision in your next project could remove the largest future risk?

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.1›Secure Software Development Life Cycle
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Secure Software Development Life Cycle

Integrate security from planning through maintenance so you catch risks early and reduce remediation cost. This board follows a practical path: requirements, design, development, testing, deployment, and maintenance.

16:9 HD Classroom
Orientation
This lesson emphasizes a proactive security mindset. You will see how early security decisions affect later testing and deployment, and how threat modeling guides design choices that lower overall risk.
Why it matters
Fixing a design-level flaw after deployment can cost many times more than addressing it in requirements. SSDLC reduces this overhead and prevents gaps that attackers exploit.
Scope
We cover security requirements, threat modeling using STRIDE and DREAD, secure design principles, secure coding practices, and code review approaches.
SSDLC visual
Concept cards connect requirements, design, code, test, deploy, maintain.
Quick example
Define a credential protection requirement during planning, validate it in design by threat modeling, enforce it with secure code, and verify via static and dynamic tests before deployment.
Common mistake: treating SSDLC as a one-time checklist rather than a continuous, evolving process tied to testing and incident feedback.
Explore Key Topics
Shift Left
Move security into requirements and design to reduce remediation cost and rework.
Threat Modeling
Use STRIDE or DREAD to identify threats and shape mitigations in architecture.
Testing & Maintenance
Static, dynamic, and interactive tests plus continuous monitoring keep systems secure over time.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this first learning block, you will explain the SSDLC and why shifting security left reduces cost and risk. You will describe how to translate data sensitivity and compliance needs into security requirements that guide design and testing. You will identify where threat modeling fits in design and how STRIDE helps categorize threats so a team can propose focused mitigations. Finally, you will perform a basic threat modeling exercise for a simple feature and propose pragmatic mitigations. For example, when you list assets for a photo-sharing app, calling out user credentials and photo storage early lets you specify encryption and access controls during planning rather than scrambling after a breach. A common misconception is that compliance equals security; compliance addresses specific controls but does not replace proactive threat discovery. Each objective here includes a milestone that verifies you can apply the skill, such as writing a security requirement or mapping STRIDE threats to a data flow. These skills change how teams plan, design, and test software so that security becomes a predictable part of delivery.

screens.title: SSDLC and the 'Shift Left' Principle
screens.narratorSegment: The SSDLC frames security as an ongoing, integrated set of activities across the full development lifecycle. At its heart is the 'shift left' principle: move security considerations earlier into planning and design so that controls are designed in, not bolted on. This matters because the cost and effort to remediate vulnerabilities grows as a project progresses. A design-level flaw may be inexpensive to change in architecture, but the same flaw fixed in production could trigger rework across code, tests, and live data migrations. A concrete example is an authentication requirement. If the team defines credential protection in requirements, design can include session handling and storage controls. Those decisions make it straightforward for developers to implement and for testers to validate. A common misconception is that shifting left simply means more static analysis. In fact, shift left is cultural: it requires planners, architects, developers, and security specialists to collaborate early. That collaboration produces clear security requirements, reduced rework, and a predictable plan for testing and deployment. Reflect: on your next feature, what single security decision could you move into requirements to reduce downstream cost?

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.1›Shift Left
Core Concept

Move security earlier to reduce cost and uncertainty

Shifting left means asking security questions during requirements and design so remediations are cheaper and fewer changes are needed later.

Definition
SSDLC: an SDLC extension where security activities are integrated into each phase, with emphasis on earlier phases through shift left.
Concrete example
Specify credential protection in requirements so design includes storage and session controls. This reduces rework during testing and deployment.
Why this changes outcomes
  • Early design choices set constraints that simplify secure implementation and testing.
  • Clear security requirements reduce ambiguity and surface compliance needs before coding begins.
  • Team collaboration minimizes late-stage surprises and costly rework.
Misconception
Shift left is not only running more static scans; it is about early decisions and shared responsibility.
Check
Ask whether your next project will set security decisions in requirements or wait until testing to discover them.
Key Takeaway

Shifting left saves effort because architecture-level controls are cheaper to design than to retrofit.

screens.title: Security Requirements in the Requirements Phase
screens.narratorSegment: Security requirements are explicit non-functional constraints that describe how an application must protect data, maintain integrity, and resist attacks. Good requirements are measurable, tied to assets, and reflect regulatory obligations and abuse cases. For example, instead of the vague requirement 'users can log in', a security requirement says 'the system must enforce a minimum password length and complexity, rotate credentials periodically, and store passwords using an approved cryptographic hash with salt'. This level of detail guides architecture and tells developers and testers what success looks like. A practical approach is to enumerate assets—user credentials, user photos, metadata, databases, and storage—and then pair each asset with security controls such as access controls, encryption, and retention policies. Common mistakes include writing requirements that are too general, or writing only compliance checkboxes without addressing the real threats. A good requirement also defines verification: how will you test it in SAST, DAST, or acceptance tests? Closing question: which asset in your next feature deserves the most specific protection and how would you measure it? Security Requirements in the Requirements Phase means write measurable security requirements tied to assets and verification methods so architecture and testing can enforce them.. In practical terms, turning data sensitivity, compliance, and abuse cases into actionable requirements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.1›Security Requirements
Definition

Measurable, asset-focused requirements

Requirements specify protection for assets, state how to verify controls, and reflect compliance or abuse-case needs.

Asset list example
  • User credentials (hashed)
  • User photos (stored in cloud storage)
  • Application database and metadata
Requirement example
The system must enforce password length and complexity, rotate credentials as required, and store credentials using a salted cryptographic hash. Verification: static analysis for use of approved hashing APIs and an integration test that validates login failure on tampered credentials.
Process: turn assets into requirements
  1. Identify primary assets and their sensitivity.
  2. List entry points and trust boundaries that affect those assets.
  3. Write measurable requirements tied to assets and verification approaches.
  4. Record acceptance criteria for testing and compliance checks.
Common Mistake
Writing vague or checklist-style requirements that do not tell implementers how to verify or enforce a control.
Key Takeaway

Security requirements must be measurable, asset-focused, and include verification so design and testing can act on them.

screens.title: Threat Modeling in the Design Phase (STRIDE & DREAD)
screens.narratorSegment: Threat modeling is the structured activity that exposes where attackers might target an application. It belongs in the design phase so architects can trade off mitigations against functional needs. Two helpful methodologies are STRIDE and DREAD. STRIDE gives categories: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege; using these letters you check each data flow and component for relevant threats. DREAD is an earlier scoring rubric that considers damage, reproducibility, exploitability, affected users, and discoverability to prioritize issues. A simple exercise is a login and photo upload data flow: list assets, draw trust boundaries at the browser, A P I, and storage layers, then apply STRIDE to each flow. For example, information disclosure against photo storage suggests encryption-at-rest; spoofing against login suggests multi-factor or robust credential verification. Misconception: threat modeling is not a one-person checklist. It benefits from cross-functional participation so developers, designers, and security staff agree on risk and viable mitigations. Final thought: what trust boundary in your system could expose the most sensitive data if left unprotected? Threat Modeling in the Design Phase (STRIDE & DREAD) means threat modeling uses stride and scoring to find and prioritize design-level threats; do it collaboratively at design time.. In practical terms, systematically identify threats, trust boundaries, and mitigations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.1›Threat Modeling
Process Flow

Apply STRIDE to flows and components

Identify assets, mark trust boundaries, and walk each data flow against STRIDE categories to find threats and propose mitigations.

STRIDE
Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info disclosure, DoS, Elevation of privilege
DREAD (scoring)
Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability — use to prioritize threats.
Mitigation types
Least privilege, secure defaults, defense in depth, separation of concerns, encryption.
Worked example: login + photo upload
Assets
  • User credentials
  • Uploaded photos
  • Application database and cloud storage
Entry points / trust boundaries
  • Login form (browser → API)
  • Upload API (API → storage)
  • Admin access to database
Sample STRIDE findings
  • Information disclosure on photo storage → mitigation: encrypt at rest and enforce access checks.
  • Spoofing on login → mitigation: strong credential policies and consider multi-factor.
Misconception
Threat modeling is not a one-person task or a one-time activity. It must be collaborative and revisited as design changes.
Key Takeaway

Use STRIDE to systematically find threats, then prioritize them with a scoring method and assign practical mitigations.

screens.title: Secure Design Principles
screens.narratorSegment: Secure design principles are the architectural guidelines that reduce an application's attack surface and increase resilience. Least privilege limits access to only what a component or user needs, so a compromised element has minimal reach. Defense in depth layers controls—authentication, authorization, input validation, and network controls—so that failure in one control does not lead to system compromise. Secure defaults mean systems start in a safe state and require explicit action to relax protections. Separation of concerns divides responsibilities so a vulnerability in one area does not automatically give access to another. A concrete example is separating file storage from the main application database, with the storage service enforcing its own access checks and encryption; even if the app is compromised, raw storage is not directly accessible. A frequent misconception is treating these principles as optional architecture preferences; in SSDLC they are engineering requirements that shape threat mitigations and tests. As you design, ask which combination of these principles reduces the likely impact of the threats you identified in your threat model. Secure Design Principles means apply least privilege, defense in depth, secure defaults, and separation of concerns to make designs resilient and easier to test.. In practical terms, least privilege, defense in depth, secure defaults, and separation of concerns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.1›Secure Design Principles
Definition

Architectural guidelines that reduce attack surface

Design principles guide trade-offs and ensure mitigations are feasible and testable across the lifecycle.

Least Privilege
Grant only necessary permissions to users and components to limit blast radius.
Defense in Depth
Use layered controls so one failure does not compromise the entire system.
Secure Defaults
Systems should default to the most restrictive safe configuration.
Separation of Concerns
Separate roles and components to keep failures contained and simpler to test.
Design analogy
Think of a building: least privilege is a keycard for each room; defense in depth is having locked doors, alarms, and guards. Secure defaults close doors by default, and separation of concerns keeps utilities behind separate walls.
Applied example
Place photo storage behind a service that enforces access tokens and encryption rather than letting the main app directly expose storage credentials.
Key Takeaway

Use design principles as required controls to guide architecture, implementation, and testing decisions.

screens.title: Development Phase: Secure Coding and Code Reviews
screens.narratorSegment: During development, teams implement the security requirements and design mitigations using secure coding practices. This includes choosing vetted libraries, avoiding common vulnerabilities, and following agreed coding standards. Code reviews—both manual and automated—are essential to catch logic errors, misuse of APIs, and omissions. Automated tools such as static analysis can find classes of defects quickly, but they do not replace thoughtful manual review. A concrete illustration: when implementing credential storage, developers should use the approved hashing APIs specified in requirements and include unit tests verifying salted hashes are produced. During a review, a reviewer checks that hashing is used correctly and that secrets are not logged or hard-coded. A common mistake is over-reliance on tools; static analysis finds patterns but human reviewers find design-level misuse and context-dependent errors. To make reviews practical, use small, frequent pull requests and pair reviewers with security-savy developers so feedback is timely and actionable. What's one code convention you can adopt with your team to prevent a common vulnerability? Development Phase: Secure Coding and Code Reviews means secure coding plus both automated and manual code reviews catch implementation flaws and ensure requirements are correctly implemented.. In practical terms, practical controls: secure libraries, coding standards, and peer review. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.1›Secure Coding
Process

Implement requirements with secure libraries and review

Secure coding enforces the design. Code reviews and automated analysis validate implementation and catch context-dependent issues.

Secure coding checklist
  • Use vetted libraries and avoid deprecated APIs.
  • Follow coding standards that prohibit secret leakage and unsafe memory or concurrency patterns.
  • Write unit tests that assert the security behaviors in requirements.
Code review guidance
  • Prefer small, frequent pull requests for faster, higher-quality reviews.
  • Combine automated SAST with manual review for context-sensitive checks.
  • Ensure reviewers validate that mitigations from threat models are implemented.
Concrete code example (illustrative)
// Pseudo-code to show intent, not an API
function storeCredentials(username, password) {
  salt = generateRandomSalt()
  hashed = hashFunction(password + salt)
  saveToDatabase(username, hashed, salt)
}

// Verification unit test
assert(checkLogin('alice','wrong') == false)
Note: the example shows producing a salted hash and verifying behavior in tests. The specific approved hashing API should be defined in requirements.
Common Mistake
Relying solely on automated analysis and skipping human reviews that catch context and design misuse.
Key Takeaway

Pair secure coding with automated and manual review; use tests that verify security requirements are actually met.

screens.title: Security Testing Techniques: SAST, DAST, IAST, and Pen Testing
screens.narratorSegment: Security testing is not a single tool; it’s an ensemble. Static application security testing, or SAST, analyzes source code or compiled artifacts without running the program. It helps you find coding mistakes like unsafe string handling or missing input validation early. Dynamic application security testing, or DAST, exercises a running application by sending inputs and observing behavior; it finds runtime issues such as authentication bypasses or unescaped output that SAST might miss. Interactive application security testing, IAST, blends both: it observes code execution from inside during tests to give higher-fidelity findings. Finally, penetration testing simulates an attacker with human creativity to chain issues together and show real impact. A concrete example: a SAST rule might flag an unparameterized S Q L call in code. DAST could then demonstrate that an input actually allows a crafted payload to reach the database. IAST can confirm which lines executed during the test and help prioritize the fix. A common misconception is that running a single scanner is enough. Each tool has blind spots; SAST misses runtime misconfiguration, DAST can miss low-frequency code paths, and IAST needs representative tests. The practical approach is layered testing: use SAST during development, IAST in QA, DAST and targeted penetration tests against staging, and repeat after deployment. This layered strategy reduces late discovery costs and gives a clearer picture of risk. Consider, after your next sprint, running an automated SAST scan, adding IAST hooks to your QA pipeline, and scheduling a short pen-test sprint to validate the most critical flows. What testing mix will best expose the high-risk areas in your application?

It helps you find coding mistakes like unsafe string handling or missing input validation early. Dynamic application security testing, or DAST, exercises a running application by sending inputs and observing behavior; it finds runtime issues such as authentication bypasses or unescaped output that SAST might miss. Interactive application security testing, IAST, blends both: it observes code execution from inside during tests to give higher-fidelity findings. Finally, penetration testing simulates an attacker with human creativity to chain issues together and show real impact. A concrete example: a SAST rule might flag an unparameterized S Q L call in code. DAST could then demonstrate that an input actually allows a crafted payload to reach the database. IAST can confirm which lines executed during the test and help prioritize the fix. A common misconception is that running a single scanner is enough. Each tool has blind spots; SAST misses runtime misconfiguration, DAST can miss low-frequency code paths, and IAST needs representative tests. The practical approach is layered testing: use SAST during development, IAST in QA, DAST and targeted penetration tests against staging, and repeat after deployment. This layered strategy reduces late discovery costs and gives a clearer picture of risk. Consider, after your next sprint, running an automated SAST scan, adding IAST hooks to your QA pipeline, and scheduling a short pen-test sprint to validate the most critical flows. What testing mix will best expose the high-risk areas in your application?

keyIdea.title: Layered testing catches different flaws
keyIdea.text: Use SAST early, IAST during QA, DAST and pen tests in staging to cover code and runtime gaps.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Security Testing Techniques
Testing Overview

No single test covers everything. Combine static, dynamic, interactive, and manual testing to detect code, runtime, and chained attack scenarios.

SAST
DAST
IAST
Scanner Comparison
SAST: Code-level checks

Static analysis flags insecure patterns before running code. Best for early fixes and IDE integration.

DAST: Black-box runtime checks

Tests run against the service to find runtime misconfigurations and input handling flaws.

IAST: Observes inside tests

Combines runtime info and code paths to reduce false positives and highlight real impact.

Example: SQL Injection Detection Flow
SAST finds
// flagged by SAST
String query = "SELECT * FROM photos WHERE ownerId = '" + userId + "'";
execute(query);

SAST flags concatenation that could allow injection if inputs are untrusted.

DAST confirms

DAST sends a crafted payload to the upload endpoint and shows a failure or unexpected output, proving exploitation at runtime.

Common Mistake

Relying on one scanner creates blind spots. Combine tools and add human review for complex flows.

Key Takeaway

Layer testing across SDLC phases: SAST in development, IAST in QA, DAST and pen tests in staging to validate real-world impact.

Try This

Add an automated SAST run to your CI pipeline and schedule a focused DAST scan for the latest build before release.

screens.title: Deployment Hardening: Secure Configuration and Access Controls
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment is where code meets infrastructure, and small configuration errors can expose the entire system. Hardening means reducing the attack surface: remove unused services, enforce secure defaults, and close open ports. Access control must be principle-based—apply least privilege for service accounts, CI/CD pipelines, and administrators. Use configuration as code so environment settings are reviewable and versioned. For example, a container image should run with a non-root user, have only required capabilities, and use read-only filesystem mounts where possible. A common deployment mistake is leaving default credentials or permissive storage buckets. Another is trusting the pipeline implicitly; the pipeline itself should have restricted credentials and signed artifacts. Use automated checks in your deployment pipeline to validate configuration rules, such as disallowing deployments with exposed debug flags or open database ports. Also, secure secrets: do not bake credentials into images or code. Instead, use a secrets manager with fine-grained access and rotation policies. Finally, enforce runtime controls like web application firewalls, network segmentation, and runtime monitoring to detect misuse. Remember that secure deployment is an extension of design and development choices; it can mitigate many issues but cannot fix fundamentally insecure design. As you prepare your next release, validate deployment templates, rotate secrets, and verify the pipeline has least privilege. What single configuration check would most reduce risk in your current environment?

Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Deployment Hardening
Core Controls for Deployment Security
  • Use configuration-as-code to version and review environment settings.
  • Enforce least privilege on service accounts and CI/CD credentials.
  • Protect secrets with a dedicated secrets manager and rotate regularly.
  • Harden images: non-root users, minimal packages, capabilities removed.
  • Validate runtime settings: firewall rules, TLS, storage permissions.
Pipeline Hardening Checklist
Signed build artifacts
Least-privilege deploy role
Secrets not in code
Config validation gates
Concrete Example

A container image was running as root and exposed SSH by default. By switching to a non-root user, removing SSH, and setting a read-only filesystem, the attack surface was reduced and the team met compliance requirements.

Pro Tip

Add automated configuration checks in CI that fail the pipeline when insecure settings are detected. Treat configuration drift like code debt.

Key Takeaway

Secure deployment requires intentional controls: secrets management, least privilege, image hardening, and pipeline validation.

screens.title: Ongoing Security: Monitoring, Vulnerability Management, and Patching
screens.narratorSegment: Security doesn't end at deployment. Maintenance is a continuous cycle of observation, triage, and remediation. Monitoring collects telemetry—logs, alerts, metrics—from applications, containers, and infrastructure to surface anomalies that might indicate an incident. Vulnerability management means regularly scanning dependencies and environments for known CVEs, assessing severity, and scheduling fixes. Patching must be prioritized: critical remote code execution or privilege escalation issues get fast-track response, while lower-severity items follow a regular release cadence. A concrete example: a third-party image library releases a critical patch. The team identifies usages via SBOM or dependency scans, runs a quick integration test, and deploys a hotfix to staging, followed by production rollout with a rollback plan. Misconceptions arise when teams equate patching with a single update; in reality it is triage plus verification. Also watch for regressions—rigorous testing and canary rollouts help. Use automated alerting tied to your vulnerability scanner so new CVEs generate tracked remediation tickets. Post-deployment, integrate telemetry with your incident response: an alert from a runtime detection rule should feed a ticket with context and a suggested remediation. Continuous improvement means learning from incidents, updating threat models, and adjusting controls. As a next step, ensure your backlog includes prioritized CVE fixes and a runbook for emergency patches. How will you reduce the time from discovery to verified deployment in your workflow?

keyIdea.text: Combine monitoring, prioritized patching, and verification to keep the application resilient as threats evolve.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Maintenance & Patching
Maintenance Workflow
1. Monitor
Collect logs and alerts to detect anomalies.
2. Discover
Find vulnerabilities via scanners and SBOM analysis.
3. Triage
Prioritize by impact, exploitability, and exposure.
4. Remediate
Patch, test, deploy, and verify; document the change.
Concrete Patch Example

A dependency has a critical CVE. Use SBOM to find affected services, create a patch branch, run automated tests, deploy to canary, monitor for regressions for one hour, then roll forward to production. If a regression appears, immediately rollback and open a postmortem ticket.

Verification checklist
  • Automated tests passed for canary
  • No increase in error rates or latency
  • Deployment artifacts signed and logged
Pitfall

Delaying patches because they are inconvenient or untested increases exposure. Prioritize critical fixes and make testing fast.

Key Takeaway

Automate detection, prioritize by risk, and verify patches with canaries and monitoring to reduce incident windows.

screens.title: Implementation Anti-patterns and How They Damage SSDLC
screens.narratorSegment: Even well-intentioned teams fall into anti-patterns that weaken the SSDLC. One anti-pattern is treating security as a checkbox — doing a one-off audit and calling the project secure. This produces a false sense of safety because new code, dependencies, and configurations change risk quickly. Another is involving security too late; developers then face expensive rework. A third mistake is failing to train developers on secure coding practices, which lets repeatable mistakes persist. Consider the real-world contrast: a team that shifts left and integrates SAST catches parameterization issues before build, while a team that waits for testing discovers the same flaw in staging, requiring emergency fixes and possible rollbacks. Fixing these anti-patterns requires cultural and process changes: embed security requirements in planning, include security experts in design sessions, and invest in developer training and actionable tooling. Use metrics that matter—time to remediate critical findings, percentage of builds blocked by policy violations, and mean time to detect anomalous behavior. A useful habit is to schedule periodic SSDLC retrospectives: review incidents, update threat models, and prioritize automation gaps. Misconceptions to watch for include assuming tools will educate developers automatically; tools highlight problems, but training and code review build capability. To make progress, start with one measurable change this quarter: either add a policy gate in CI, run a monthly pen test against a high-risk service, or deliver a secure-coding workshop. Which corrective action will you commit to this sprint?

Anti-patterns
  • Checkbox Security: One audit and no follow-up.
  • Late Security Involvement: Design flaws found during testing.
  • No Developer Training: Repeatable coding mistakes persist.
Corrective Practices
Embed security in requirements and acceptance criteria
Policy-gate critical checks in CI/CD
Deliver targeted secure-coding workshops
Metric-driven Improvement

Track time to remediate critical vulnerabilities, percent of builds blocked by security policy, and frequency of repeat findings. Use those metrics in retrospectives to prioritize tooling, training, and design reviews.

Playbook Item

Run an SSDLC retrospective after each incident: update threat models, close tooling gaps, and schedule developer training.

Key Takeaway

Anti-patterns are fixable through process, measurement, and education. Make small, measurable commitments each sprint.

screens.title: Basic Threat Modeling Exercise Walkthrough (Photo Sharing App)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk a practical threat-modeling exercise using STRIDE for a photo sharing application with authentication and an upload A P I. First, identify assets: user credentials, stored photos, metadata, database, web and application servers, and cloud storage. Entry points include the login form, registration form, upload endpoint, and photo viewing endpoints. Now apply STRIDE to the authentication feature: Spoofing could let an attacker impersonate a user; mitigation is multi-factor authentication and strong password hashing. Tampering could alter session tokens or requests; mitigation includes signed session tokens, CSRF protections, and input validation. Repudiation concerns require logging and non-repudiation controls, so add tamper-evident audit logs. Information disclosure affects sensitive profile data; mitigate with encryption in transit and at rest and strict access controls. Denial of service could target login endpoints; use rate limiting and WAF rules. Elevation of privilege could be a weak role assignment on registration; mitigate with strict role enforcement and separation of duties. For photo upload, STRIDE finds tampering via malicious file types, information disclosure through improperly set bucket permissions, and injection risks if metadata is processed without sanitization. Mitigations include validating file types, scanning uploads for malware, enforcing signed URLs and least-privilege storage roles, and normalizing metadata. A common misconception is that threat models require exhaustive lists; instead, focus on highest-value assets and most probable attack paths first. As an action: create a short STRIDE table for the upload flow, list top three threats, and pick one mitigation to implement this sprint. Which threat will you block first?

Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › Threat Modeling Exercise
Assets & Entry Points
  • Assets: User credentials, photos, metadata, DB, web server, cloud storage.
  • Entry Points: Login form, register form, upload API, view API.
STRIDE Table (sample rows)
Spoofing — attacker uses stolen credentials. Mitigation: MFA, strong hashing, monitor logins.
Tampering — malicious upload modifies stored files. Mitigation: content scanning, integrity checks.
Information Disclosure — public bucket exposes private photos. Mitigation: signed URLs, least-privilege storage roles.
Example: Upload Flow Mitigations
  1. Validate file type and size server-side; reject suspicious content.
  2. Store uploads in a private bucket with signed URL access.
  3. Scan files for malware as part of processing pipeline.
  4. Log upload actions with user ID and request context for non-repudiation.
Exercise

Draft a STRIDE row for the login endpoint, pick the top two threats, and propose a mitigation you can implement this sprint.

Key Takeaway

Threat modeling turns abstract risk into prioritized actions. Start small, focus on high-value assets, and iterate.

screens.narratorSegment: Here are the essential ideas to retain. First, SSDLC integrates security throughout every SDLC phase so security is proactive rather than reactive. This lowers cost and risk by catching issues earlier. Second, shift left means bringing security into requirements and design so controls are built in, not grafted on later. Third, threat modeling is a structured way to identify attackers, assets, and attack paths; STRIDE is a common methodology that helps you categorize and mitigate threats. Fourth, security must be layered: secure design, secure coding, and multiple testing techniques work together. Finally, deployment and maintenance are ongoing responsibilities — configuration, secrets management, monitoring, and timely patching are essential. fullNarratorScript:
We begin by treating security as an integral part of software design rather than an add-on. The Secure Software Development Life Cycle, or SSDLC, shifts security left so that concerns like data protection, threat modeling, and secure defaults are considered from the first requirement and design discussions. This reduces cost and risk because vulnerabilities discovered early are cheaper and simpler to fix than those found in production. In this lesson you will learn what it means to shift left, how to define security requirements that capture data sensitivity and regulatory needs, how designers can apply threat modeling techniques to anticipate attacks, and how development and testing practices catch issues before deployment. A practical example is defining a credential-protection requirement during planning and confirming it in design through threat modeling; that single early decision saves time in later code reviews and penetration testing. A common misconception is that adding a security team late in the cycle is sufficient. In practice, late involvement often creates rework and missed controls. As you go through these screens, ask yourself: which early decision in your next project could remove the largest future risk?

By the end of this first learning block, you will explain the SSDLC and why shifting security left reduces cost and risk. You will describe how to translate data sensitivity and compliance needs into security requirements that guide design and testing. You will identify where threat modeling fits in design and how STRIDE helps categorize threats so a team can propose focused mitigations. Finally, you will perform a basic threat modeling exercise for a simple feature and propose pragmatic mitigations. For example, when you list assets for a photo-sharing app, calling out user credentials and photo storage early lets you specify encryption and access controls during planning rather than scrambling after a breach. A common misconception is that compliance equals security; compliance addresses specific controls but does not replace proactive threat discovery. Each objective here includes a milestone that verifies you can apply the skill, such as writing a security requirement or mapping STRIDE threats to a data flow. These skills change how teams plan, design, and test software so that security becomes a predictable part of delivery.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and integration. You will learn to incorporate security requirements into project planning artifacts and to ensure designers and security engineers collaborate on threat models. You will practice applying STRIDE to real features and mapping each threat to one or more mitigation strategies. You will learn basic metrics to decide when to escalate an issue to a formal penetration test or incident response exercise. For example, after defining assets and trust boundaries for a photo upload feature, you should be able to produce a short table mapping spoofing or information disclosure to concrete controls such as multi-factor verification or encrypted storage. A misconception to guard against is equating testing coverage with total security; tests find classes of issues but do not guarantee absence of design-level flaws. Each card here includes a verified milestone such as producing a threat model or embedding a security requirement into a user story, which ensures these skills translate into team practice.

The SSDLC frames security as an ongoing, integrated set of activities across the full development lifecycle. At its heart is the 'shift left' principle: move security considerations earlier into planning and design so that controls are designed in, not bolted on. This matters because the cost and effort to remediate vulnerabilities grows as a project progresses. A design-level flaw may be inexpensive to change in architecture, but the same flaw fixed in production could trigger rework across code, tests, and live data migrations. A concrete example is an authentication requirement. If the team defines credential protection in requirements, design can include session handling and storage controls. Those decisions make it straightforward for developers to implement and for testers to validate. A common misconception is that shifting left simply means more static analysis. In fact, shift left is cultural: it requires planners, architects, developers, and security specialists to collaborate early. That collaboration produces clear security requirements, reduced rework, and a predictable plan for testing and deployment. Reflect: on your next feature, what single security decision could you move into requirements to reduce downstream cost?

Security requirements are explicit non-functional constraints that describe how an application must protect data, maintain integrity, and resist attacks. Good requirements are measurable, tied to assets, and reflect regulatory obligations and abuse cases. For example, instead of the vague requirement 'users can log in', a security requirement says 'the system must enforce a minimum password length and complexity, rotate credentials periodically, and store passwords using an approved cryptographic hash with salt'. This level of detail guides architecture and tells developers and testers what success looks like. A practical approach is to enumerate assets—user credentials, user photos, metadata, databases, and storage—and then pair each asset with security controls such as access controls, encryption, and retention policies. Common mistakes include writing requirements that are too general, or writing only compliance checkboxes without addressing the real threats. A good requirement also defines verification: how will you test it in SAST, DAST, or acceptance tests? Closing question: which asset in your next feature deserves the most specific protection and how would you measure it? Security Requirements in the Requirements Phase means write measurable security requirements tied to assets and verification methods so architecture and testing can enforce them.. In practical terms, turning data sensitivity, compliance, and abuse cases into actionable requirements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Threat modeling is the structured activity that exposes where attackers might target an application. It belongs in the design phase so architects can trade off mitigations against functional needs. Two helpful methodologies are STRIDE and DREAD. STRIDE gives categories: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege; using these letters you check each data flow and component for relevant threats. DREAD is an earlier scoring rubric that considers damage, reproducibility, exploitability, affected users, and discoverability to prioritize issues. A simple exercise is a login and photo upload data flow: list assets, draw trust boundaries at the browser, A P I, and storage layers, then apply STRIDE to each flow. For example, information disclosure against photo storage suggests encryption-at-rest; spoofing against login suggests multi-factor or robust credential verification. Misconception: threat modeling is not a one-person checklist. It benefits from cross-functional participation so developers, designers, and security staff agree on risk and viable mitigations. Final thought: what trust boundary in your system could expose the most sensitive data if left unprotected? Threat Modeling in the Design Phase (STRIDE & DREAD) means threat modeling uses stride and scoring to find and prioritize design-level threats; do it collaboratively at design time.. In practical terms, systematically identify threats, trust boundaries, and mitigations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Secure design principles are the architectural guidelines that reduce an application's attack surface and increase resilience. Least privilege limits access to only what a component or user needs, so a compromised element has minimal reach. Defense in depth layers controls—authentication, authorization, input validation, and network controls—so that failure in one control does not lead to system compromise. Secure defaults mean systems start in a safe state and require explicit action to relax protections. Separation of concerns divides responsibilities so a vulnerability in one area does not automatically give access to another. A concrete example is separating file storage from the main application database, with the storage service enforcing its own access checks and encryption; even if the app is compromised, raw storage is not directly accessible. A frequent misconception is treating these principles as optional architecture preferences; in SSDLC they are engineering requirements that shape threat mitigations and tests. As you design, ask which combination of these principles reduces the likely impact of the threats you identified in your threat model. Secure Design Principles means apply least privilege, defense in depth, secure defaults, and separation of concerns to make designs resilient and easier to test.. In practical terms, least privilege, defense in depth, secure defaults, and separation of concerns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

During development, teams implement the security requirements and design mitigations using secure coding practices. This includes choosing vetted libraries, avoiding common vulnerabilities, and following agreed coding standards. Code reviews—both manual and automated—are essential to catch logic errors, misuse of APIs, and omissions. Automated tools such as static analysis can find classes of defects quickly, but they do not replace thoughtful manual review. A concrete illustration: when implementing credential storage, developers should use the approved hashing APIs specified in requirements and include unit tests verifying salted hashes are produced. During a review, a reviewer checks that hashing is used correctly and that secrets are not logged or hard-coded. A common mistake is over-reliance on tools; static analysis finds patterns but human reviewers find design-level misuse and context-dependent errors. To make reviews practical, use small, frequent pull requests and pair reviewers with security-savy developers so feedback is timely and actionable. What's one code convention you can adopt with your team to prevent a common vulnerability? Development Phase: Secure Coding and Code Reviews means secure coding plus both automated and manual code reviews catch implementation flaws and ensure requirements are correctly implemented.. In practical terms, practical controls: secure libraries, coding standards, and peer review. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Security testing is not a single tool; it’s an ensemble. Static application security testing, or SAST, analyzes source code or compiled artifacts without running the program. It helps you find coding mistakes like unsafe string handling or missing input validation early. Dynamic application security testing, or DAST, exercises a running application by sending inputs and observing behavior; it finds runtime issues such as authentication bypasses or unescaped output that SAST might miss. Interactive application security testing, IAST, blends both: it observes code execution from inside during tests to give higher-fidelity findings. Finally, penetration testing simulates an attacker with human creativity to chain issues together and show real impact. A concrete example: a SAST rule might flag an unparameterized S Q L call in code. DAST could then demonstrate that an input actually allows a crafted payload to reach the database. IAST can confirm which lines executed during the test and help prioritize the fix. A common misconception is that running a single scanner is enough. Each tool has blind spots; SAST misses runtime misconfiguration, DAST can miss low-frequency code paths, and IAST needs representative tests. The practical approach is layered testing: use SAST during development, IAST in QA, DAST and targeted penetration tests against staging, and repeat after deployment. This layered strategy reduces late discovery costs and gives a clearer picture of risk. Consider, after your next sprint, running an automated SAST scan, adding IAST hooks to your QA pipeline, and scheduling a short pen-test sprint to validate the most critical flows. What testing mix will best expose the high-risk areas in your application?

Deployment is where code meets infrastructure, and small configuration errors can expose the entire system. Hardening means reducing the attack surface: remove unused services, enforce secure defaults, and close open ports. Access control must be principle-based—apply least privilege for service accounts, CI/CD pipelines, and administrators. Use configuration as code so environment settings are reviewable and versioned. For example, a container image should run with a non-root user, have only required capabilities, and use read-only filesystem mounts where possible. A common deployment mistake is leaving default credentials or permissive storage buckets. Another is trusting the pipeline implicitly; the pipeline itself should have restricted credentials and signed artifacts. Use automated checks in your deployment pipeline to validate configuration rules, such as disallowing deployments with exposed debug flags or open database ports. Also, secure secrets: do not bake credentials into images or code. Instead, use a secrets manager with fine-grained access and rotation policies. Finally, enforce runtime controls like web application firewalls, network segmentation, and runtime monitoring to detect misuse. Remember that secure deployment is an extension of design and development choices; it can mitigate many issues but cannot fix fundamentally insecure design. As you prepare your next release, validate deployment templates, rotate secrets, and verify the pipeline has least privilege. What single configuration check would most reduce risk in your current environment?

Security doesn't end at deployment. Maintenance is a continuous cycle of observation, triage, and remediation. Monitoring collects telemetry—logs, alerts, metrics—from applications, containers, and infrastructure to surface anomalies that might indicate an incident. Vulnerability management means regularly scanning dependencies and environments for known CVEs, assessing severity, and scheduling fixes. Patching must be prioritized: critical remote code execution or privilege escalation issues get fast-track response, while lower-severity items follow a regular release cadence. A concrete example: a third-party image library releases a critical patch. The team identifies usages via SBOM or dependency scans, runs a quick integration test, and deploys a hotfix to staging, followed by production rollout with a rollback plan. Misconceptions arise when teams equate patching with a single update; in reality it is triage plus verification. Also watch for regressions—rigorous testing and canary rollouts help. Use automated alerting tied to your vulnerability scanner so new CVEs generate tracked remediation tickets. Post-deployment, integrate telemetry with your incident response: an alert from a runtime detection rule should feed a ticket with context and a suggested remediation. Continuous improvement means learning from incidents, updating threat models, and adjusting controls. As a next step, ensure your backlog includes prioritized CVE fixes and a runbook for emergency patches. How will you reduce the time from discovery to verified deployment in your workflow?

Even well-intentioned teams fall into anti-patterns that weaken the SSDLC. One anti-pattern is treating security as a checkbox — doing a one-off audit and calling the project secure. This produces a false sense of safety because new code, dependencies, and configurations change risk quickly. Another is involving security too late; developers then face expensive rework. A third mistake is failing to train developers on secure coding practices, which lets repeatable mistakes persist. Consider the real-world contrast: a team that shifts left and integrates SAST catches parameterization issues before build, while a team that waits for testing discovers the same flaw in staging, requiring emergency fixes and possible rollbacks. Fixing these anti-patterns requires cultural and process changes: embed security requirements in planning, include security experts in design sessions, and invest in developer training and actionable tooling. Use metrics that matter—time to remediate critical findings, percentage of builds blocked by policy violations, and mean time to detect anomalous behavior. A useful habit is to schedule periodic SSDLC retrospectives: review incidents, update threat models, and prioritize automation gaps. Misconceptions to watch for include assuming tools will educate developers automatically; tools highlight problems, but training and code review build capability. To make progress, start with one measurable change this quarter: either add a policy gate in CI, run a monthly pen test against a high-risk service, or deliver a secure-coding workshop. Which corrective action will you commit to this sprint?

Let's walk a practical threat-modeling exercise using STRIDE for a photo sharing application with authentication and an upload A P I. First, identify assets: user credentials, stored photos, metadata, database, web and application servers, and cloud storage. Entry points include the login form, registration form, upload endpoint, and photo viewing endpoints. Now apply STRIDE to the authentication feature: Spoofing could let an attacker impersonate a user; mitigation is multi-factor authentication and strong password hashing. Tampering could alter session tokens or requests; mitigation includes signed session tokens, CSRF protections, and input validation. Repudiation concerns require logging and non-repudiation controls, so add tamper-evident audit logs. Information disclosure affects sensitive profile data; mitigate with encryption in transit and at rest and strict access controls. Denial of service could target login endpoints; use rate limiting and WAF rules. Elevation of privilege could be a weak role assignment on registration; mitigate with strict role enforcement and separation of duties. For photo upload, STRIDE finds tampering via malicious file types, information disclosure through improperly set bucket permissions, and injection risks if metadata is processed without sanitization. Mitigations include validating file types, scanning uploads for malware, enforcing signed URLs and least-privilege storage roles, and normalizing metadata. A common misconception is that threat models require exhaustive lists; instead, focus on highest-value assets and most probable attack paths first. As an action: create a short STRIDE table for the upload flow, list top three threats, and pick one mitigation to implement this sprint. Which threat will you block first?

Here are the essential ideas to retain. First, SSDLC integrates security throughout every SDLC phase so security is proactive rather than reactive. This lowers cost and risk by catching issues earlier. Second, shift left means bringing security into requirements and design so controls are built in, not grafted on later. Third, threat modeling is a structured way to identify attackers, assets, and attack paths; STRIDE is a common methodology that helps you categorize and mitigate threats. Fourth, security must be layered: secure design, secure coding, and multiple testing techniques work together. Finally, deployment and maintenance are ongoing responsibilities — configuration, secrets management, monitoring, and timely patching are essential. Keep these short statements as practical anchors when you review designs, prepare tests, or schedule releases. Which of these concepts will you prioritize in your next planning meeting?

Keep these practical reminders close. First, use layered testing—SAST for code, IAST for runtime insight, DAST for black-box checks, and pen tests to show real impact. Second, secure deployment practices like configuration as code, secrets management, and least privilege reduce runtime exposure. Third, maintenance must include telemetry, prioritized patching, and verification steps such as canary rollouts. Fourth, avoid anti-patterns: do not treat SSDLC as a checklist, involve security early, and train developers. Lastly, threat modeling is a prioritized activity: focus on high-value assets and most probable attack paths and iterate. These short rules guide day-to-day decisions and help you measure security improvements over time. Which reminder will you act on first?
